```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(PharmaStatsR)
```

## Validate schema

```{r}
df <- data.frame(
  SubjectID = c(1L, 1L, 2L),
  Time = c(0, 1, 0),
  DV = c(1.1, 1.2, 1.3),
  WT = c(70, 70, 80)
)
validate_data_schema(df)
```

This checks the table structure: unique, nonempty column names, integer
`SubjectID`, real numeric `Time` and `DV`, and at least one covariate. It allows
missing observations. Each preprocessing function separately validates the
variables it uses; passing the schema check does not make every column suitable
for every method.

## Impute missing values

```{r}
df2 <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, NA, 3),
  y = c(NA, 4, 5)
)
imputed <- impute_mean(df2, c("x", "y"))
imputed_median <- impute_median(df2, c("x", "y"))
```

Mean and median imputation accept real numeric vectors. Both treat `NA` and
`NaN` as missing, reject infinite values, and leave observed values unchanged.
Constant columns with at least one observation can be imputed. An entirely
missing target remains unchanged with a warning because there is no observed
value from which to estimate a replacement. Empty tables remain unchanged.

Selected variable names must be unique, present in the data, and nonmissing.
Factor, character, logical, matrix, and list columns are not numeric imputation
targets. Use an empty selection (`character(0)`) to leave the data unchanged.

### Reuse training replacements

Split data first, then fit mean or median replacements on training rows only:

```{r}
training <- data.frame(x = c(1, NA, 3, 8))
validation <- data.frame(x = c(NA, 100, NaN))
params <- fit_imputation(training, "x")
params
apply_imputation(validation, params)
```

The saved training mean is 4. The validation value 100 does not influence it.
Use `method = "median"` to save the observed training median, 3. The parameter
table can be saved with `saveRDS()` and loaded with `readRDS()`. Entirely missing
selected training columns raise an error; new columns may be entirely missing.
Both functions use literal variable names and reject infinite selected values.

To combine imputation and scaling, fit both on the same training population:

```{r}
completed_training <- apply_imputation(training, params)
scaling <- center_scale(completed_training, "x")
apply_center_scale(apply_imputation(validation, params), scaling$params)
```

For cross-validation, fit a separate imputation table and scaling parameters
inside every training fold; keep repeated subjects together when holding out
new subjects. A table imputed before `screen_covariates_lasso()` is still not
re-imputed inside its internal folds. These helpers perform numeric single-value
imputation without estimating missing-data uncertainty; they do not provide
categorical encoding or a reusable nearest-neighbor model.

### Nearest-neighbor imputation within one table

`impute_ml()` supports numeric, logical, character, and factor vectors. Numeric
targets use the neighbor mean; other targets use the neighbor mode. Factors
keep their original levels, including unused levels.

```{r}
neighbors <- data.frame(
  SubjectID = c(1L, 1000L, 1000L),
  WT = c(60, 65, 80),
  group = factor(c("A", NA, "B"), levels = c("A", "B", "C"))
)
impute_ml(neighbors, "group", k = 1, predictors = "WT")
```

The `predictors` argument selects columns for neighbor distances. The example
uses only weight and returns the full table, including the unchanged subject
identifiers. With the default `predictors = NULL`, every column other than the
current target remains a predictor. Identifiers, time, and outcomes are not
automatically excluded; choose suitable predictors for your analysis explicitly.

One selection is shared across all targets. The current target is always removed
from its own predictors, so a selection such as `c("WT", "AGE", "CRCL")` can also
include target columns. Other targets are used as predictors only if included
in that selection. An explicit `character(0)` selects no predictors; targets
needing imputation remain unchanged with a warning. Complete targets do not
produce that warning. Unknown, missing, or duplicate predictor names are rejected
even when no imputation is needed. Predictor types and values are checked when
they are used; excluded columns are preserved without influencing distances.

With the default `distance = "euclidean"`, numeric predictors retain their units,
so large-scale variables can dominate the distance. Character and factor
predictors use factor codes; this imposes distances that may be inappropriate
for nominal categories. Review the predictor choices and encoding for your
analysis. Selecting columns does not change the
distance metric or standardize their values.

In Euclidean mode, missing predictors are filled internally with their encoded
column mean, or zero when entirely missing. This does not fill their missing
values in the returned table unless they are also selected targets. Infinite
target or used predictor values are rejected. An entirely missing target, or a target without
any predictor columns, remains unchanged with a warning.

`k` must be a finite positive whole number. If it exceeds the number of comparable
observed target values, all comparable donors are used. Distance ties follow
original row order; mode ties use the first value among the selected neighbors.
Targets are processed in the supplied order, so earlier imputations can affect
later ones when those targets are also selected predictors.
Euclidean distance calculation avoids overflow from squaring large values, but
truly unrepresentable distances still require rescaling the numeric predictors.

#### Mixed predictors with Gower distance

Use `distance = "gower"` for comparisons of mixed predictor types,
following the [Gower dissimilarity definition](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/cluster/html/daisy.html).

| Predictor | Contribution |
| --- | --- |
| Numeric | Absolute difference divided by the observed range |
| Ordered factor | As numeric, using the declared level scores |
| Unordered factor or character | Zero for a match, one for a mismatch |
| Logical | Symmetric match/mismatch, including a match for two `FALSE` values |

By default, the distance averages contributions with equal weights. Missing predictor
pairs are omitted; a donor with none available is excluded. Constant numeric
predictors contribute zero when observed. Ranges use all supplied rows for each
target, so this is not preprocessing fitted separately within training folds.

```{r}
mixed <- data.frame(
  target = c(10, 20, NA),
  weight = c(60, 90, 65),
  group = factor(c("A", "B", "A"))
)
impute_ml(
  mixed, "target",
  k = 1, predictors = c("weight", "group"),
  distance = "gower"
)
```

If no comparable donor exists, the target stays missing and one warning per
target reports the affected row count. Distances based on different numbers of
observed predictors are still compared directly. Review missingness and predictor
choices for the analysis; asymmetric binary treatment is not supported.
Only selected target values change in the returned table.

#### Control predictor influence

Supply named `weights` to change predictors' relative influence with either
distance. Unspecified predictors keep weight 1. Names match literal selected
column names, so their order need not match the data or `predictors`. Weights
must be finite, nonnegative numbers with unique, nonempty names. Unknown or
unselected names are rejected, even if no target values are missing.

```{r}
weighted <- data.frame(
  target = c(10, 20, NA), x = c(0, 2, 0), z = c(1, 0, 0)
)
impute_ml(weighted, "target", k = 1, predictors = c("x", "z"))
impute_ml(weighted, "target",
  k = 1, predictors = c("x", "z"),
  weights = c(z = 9)
)
impute_ml(weighted, "target",
  k = 1, predictors = c("x", "z"),
  distance = "gower", weights = c(z = 9)
)
```

With default Euclidean distance, the first donor is nearest and the missing
target becomes 10. Weighting `z` by 9 changes the Euclidean distances from 1
and 2 to 3 and 2, so the second donor supplies 20. Euclidean weights multiply
squared differences: the distance is proportional to
`sqrt(sum(weights * differences^2))`. The variables still retain their original
units and categorical encoding.

Gower uses a weighted mean of the available contributions. A missing predictor
is omitted from both the numerator and the sum of weights for that pair. In
the example, the weighted distances are 0.9 and 0.1. A donor must have at least
one jointly observed predictor with positive weight to be comparable.

Weight 0 excludes a predictor before its type or values are checked, just as
leaving it out of `predictors` does. If no positive-weight predictors remain
after excluding the current target, missing targets stay unchanged with a
warning. The same named weights are used across targets; each target is always
excluded from its own distance calculation. `weights = NULL` and `numeric(0)`
retain equal weighting.

Weights change neighbor selection, not the mean or mode of the selected donor
values. Distance ties follow original row order; mode ties use the first value
among the selected neighbors. Internal scaling
limits overflow for large weights; extreme relative scales can still lose
floating-point precision. Multiplying all predictor weights by the same
positive factor preserves their relative influence. Weights are supplied by
the caller; this function does not estimate or tune them from the data.

## Center and scale

```{r}
cs <- center_scale(imputed, c("x", "y"))
cs$data
cs$params
```

Scaling uses the observed mean and sample standard deviation. Missing values
remain missing; imputation is a separate choice:

```{r}
with_missing <- data.frame(x = c(1, NA, 3, 5))
center_scale(with_missing, "x")
```

Each selected column needs at least two observed values, a finite mean, and a
positive finite standard deviation. Constant, entirely missing, singleton,
and infinite-valued columns raise an error instead of producing invalid scaled
values. Very large or tiny finite values can also yield an unrepresentable
standard deviation; change their units before scaling. Unselected columns are
preserved.

### Reuse scaling parameters on new data

`center_scale()` estimates parameters from the supplied table. For model
evaluation, call it on the training data and pass its saved `params` to
`apply_center_scale()` for validation or future observations:

```{r}
training <- data.frame(SubjectID = 1:3, WT = c(60, 70, 80))
validation <- data.frame(SubjectID = 4:6, WT = c(90, 100, NA))
training_scaled <- center_scale(training, "WT")
validation_scaled <- apply_center_scale(validation, training_scaled$params)
training_scaled$params
validation_scaled
```

The training mean is 70 and its sample standard deviation is 10, so the
validation weights become 2, 3, and `NA`. No parameters are estimated from
validation rows. This follows the fixed centering and scaling vectors supported
by [base R's `scale()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/scale.html).

Parameter rows are matched by literal column name, so their order and the data's
column order can differ. Parameters require unique variable names, finite means,
and positive finite standard deviations. Extra parameter columns are ignored.
The result retains row order, row names, column order, and unselected columns.
Missing values remain missing. A valid empty parameter table changes nothing.

New data may have zero rows, a single row, constant columns, or entirely missing
columns: these do not require new estimates. Selected columns must still be real
numeric vectors with no infinite values. Unknown variables, invalid parameters,
and unrepresentable transformed values raise errors.

Split subjects before estimating preprocessing parameters when evaluating
models on new subjects. Repeat the fitting and application steps within each
training/validation split. The screening functions do not yet automate this
workflow. The `fit_imputation()` / `apply_imputation()` and `fit_encoding()` /
`apply_encoding()` pairs provide saved recipes for manual composition.

## Prepare a design matrix

`prepare_model_matrix()` preserves the number, order, and names of input rows,
including rows with missing values. It uses an explicit missing-value policy,
so changing the global `na.action` option does not change the returned rows.

```{r}
matrix_data <- data.frame(
  WT = c(60, NA, 80),
  group = factor(c("A", "B", NA), levels = c("A", "B", "C")),
  row.names = c("first", "second", "third")
)
design <- prepare_model_matrix(matrix_data, c("WT", "group"))
design
dim(prepare_model_matrix(matrix_data, character(0)))
```

The matrix has no intercept. Numeric covariates contribute one column;
categorical terms use R's contrast rules, with the first categorical term using
full indicator coding. Declared factor levels, including unused levels, are
preserved. Character columns derive their levels from observed values. A factor
needs at least two declared levels; a character column needs at least two
observed categories. Logical columns use `FALSE` and `TRUE` levels.

Infinite values and unsupported types such as list or matrix columns are
rejected. Constant numeric columns are allowed, and no rank check is performed
here. An empty selection produces one row per input row and zero columns.
This helper does not impute data or record an encoding recipe to apply to future
data. Use the fit/apply pair below when reusing training coding.

### Reuse training encoding on new data

`fit_encoding()` saves training levels, actual numeric coding, and matrix column
order. `apply_encoding()` preserves those columns even when a new batch has only
one known category. It does not reevaluate contrasts, so changes to R's contrast
options do not alter a saved recipe. The result is a plain numeric matrix,
without the `assign` and `contrasts` attributes from `model.matrix()`.

```{r}
encoding <- fit_encoding(matrix_data, c("WT", "group"))
future <- data.frame(WT = c(75, NA), group = c("B", NA))
apply_encoding(future, encoding)
```

The columns remain `WT`, `groupA`, `groupB`, and `groupC`. Missing rows stay in
place; a missing category makes its entire coding block missing. An observed
category absent from the training recipe raises an error. Unused levels declared
on a new factor are harmless, and new factor level order does not change coding.

Factors retain their declared training levels. Prespecify their schema or learn
it from training data; constructing factors from the full dataset before a split
can reveal held-out categories. Character training columns need two observed
categories, and factor training columns need two declared levels. Numeric inputs
stay numeric, logical inputs stay logical, and categorical inputs may be factors
or characters. An empty selection produces a zero-column matrix; empty new data
retain the saved columns. No rank check or interaction terms are added.

Fit numeric imputation, scaling, and encoding on the same training population
and apply them in that order:

```{r}
training <- data.frame(x = c(1, NA, 3, 8), group = c("A", "B", "A", "B"))
imputation <- fit_imputation(training, "x")
completed_training <- apply_imputation(training, imputation)
scaling <- center_scale(completed_training, "x")
encoding <- fit_encoding(scaling$data, c("x", "group"))
validation <- data.frame(x = c(NA, 100), group = c("B", "A"))
completed_validation <- apply_imputation(validation, imputation)
scaled_validation <- apply_center_scale(completed_validation, scaling$params)
apply_encoding(scaled_validation, encoding)
```

Refit each transformation within every training fold, keeping subjects together
when evaluating new subjects. The screening helpers do not automate this
workflow. Save a recipe with `saveRDS()` and restore it with `readRDS()`; it stores
numeric coding and schema, with no training rows or contrast functions.

By comparison, `fit_covariate_model()` excludes rows missing its response,
subject identifier, or covariates using `na.exclude`. Its fitted model retains
native `nlme` behavior, including padding residuals for excluded observations.
